section1.title: 1. It combines multiple indicators
section1.body: SIO brings retail sentiment, options hedging, volatility pressure, capital flows, credit spreads, and institutional and active-manager positioning into one framework, then converts them into a 0 to 100 score. The {{score}} reading you see now is the combined output of those signals.

section2.title: 2. Spot extremes instead of chasing the short term
section2.body: When the score falls into very low territory, fear is usually spreading. When it rises into very high territory, the market may already be overheating. The key is to watch whether conditions are moving toward a more extreme reading.

section3.title: 3. Read the market with discipline and resist fear and greed
section3.body: When markets fall hard, people instinctively want to get out. When markets surge, FOMO makes it easy to chase. SIO adds an objective, cross-indicator reference point to your decision-making.

composite.shortDescription: The Sentiment Inside Out Fear & Greed Indicator (SIO Fear & Greed Indicator) quantifies market sentiment into a score from 0 to 100. Its purpose is to gauge whether current market participants' psychology leans towards fear or greed, similar to the CNN Fear & Greed Index and the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator. It helps investors remain calm during irrational stock market volatility and avoid emotionally driven decisions like chasing highs and selling lows.

sections.title: Composite Index Explanation
sections.content: The SIO Fear & Greed Indicator is a sentiment indicator calculated from a synthesis of multiple U.S. stock market data points, represented by a score from 0 to 100. A score closer to 0 signifies extreme fear in the market, potentially indicating a higher probability of success for buying at this time. Conversely, a score closer to 100 suggests extreme greed in the market, advising against chasing further highs. Compared to the CNN Fear & Greed Index, it incorporates a more comprehensive set of indicators, including the AAII Investor Sentiment Survey results—often considered a proxy for U.S. retail investor sentiment—to more accurately reflect the long-term relationship between market sentiment and prices.

sections.title: Historical Data Review
sections.content: Historically, whenever the Sentiment Inside Out Fear & Greed Index (SIO Fear & Greed Index) reached around 10 points, it marked a bear market bottom (including the 2009 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2022 Russo-Ukrainian War). Seizing these moments presented excellent buying opportunities.

aaiiSpread.shortDescription: The AAII Investor Sentiment Survey weekly asks members their outlook for the stock market over the next six months (bullish, bearish, neutral). The Bull-Bear Spread (bullish percentage minus bearish percentage) is a common measure of retail investor sentiment.
aaiiSpread.detailDescription: This indicator looks directly at whether retail investors are leaning bullish or bearish. When everyday investors become overwhelmingly optimistic, it usually means a lot of good news has already been priced in. When bearish responses dominate, fear has often spread broadly through the market. It works as a sentiment gauge because retail positioning is one of the clearest expressions of crowd emotion, and extreme readings often show up near turning points.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: An extremely high Bull-Bear Spread (well above the historical average) usually indicates excessive market optimism and could be a potential sell signal. Conversely, an extremely low Spread (well below the historical average, even negative) indicates excessive pessimism and could be a potential buying opportunity.

cboeRatio.shortDescription: The CBOE Put/Call Ratio is an important indicator of market speculation sentiment. It calculates the ratio of traded put option contracts to call option contracts.
cboeRatio.detailDescription: This indicator shows whether the market has recently been loading up on protective puts or aggressively buying calls. A higher put/call ratio usually means investors are hedging and worrying about downside, while a lower ratio suggests they are leaning into upside bets. It is useful for reading sentiment because options markets often reveal fear and greed earlier than cash markets, and the 5-day average smooths out one-day noise.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: A high Put/Call Ratio (typically above 1) indicates investors are buying more puts for hedging or bearish bets, suggesting market fear. A low Put/Call Ratio (typically below 0.7) indicates investors are buying more calls for speculation or bullish bets, suggesting market greed. Using a 5-day average smooths the data for better trend observation.

marketMomentum.shortDescription: The Market Momentum indicator measures the S&P 500 index's position relative to its 125-day moving average (approximately the half-year line). It reflects the strength of the market's medium-term trend.
marketMomentum.detailDescription: This indicator uses price versus its long-term moving average to judge whether the market has run too far too fast in either direction. When price sits far above trend for a long stretch, chasing behavior is usually strong and the market may be overheating. When price is deeply below trend, pessimism is often already heavy. It works as a sentiment read because emotion eventually shows up in price extension: the more stretched momentum becomes, the more one-sided the crowd usually is.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: When the S&P 500 is significantly above its 125-day MA, it indicates a strong uptrend, strong momentum, and market greed. When the index is significantly below the MA, it indicates a downtrend, weak momentum, and market fear.

marginShortRatio.shortDescription: The margin short ratio compares margin lending and short-selling activity to show shifts in leverage and bearish positioning.
marginShortRatio.detailDescription: When the margin short ratio rises, it usually means short positioning is increasing relative to margin buying, which points to a more defensive or bearish crowd. When it falls, downside pressure eases and risk appetite is generally stronger. It works as a sentiment read because changes in lending and shorting behavior often show how traders are leaning before price fully reflects it.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: A higher margin short ratio usually reflects stronger bearish pressure and more cautious sentiment. A lower ratio usually reflects stronger bullish pressure and a more risk-on market.

twMarketMomentum.shortDescription: Taiwan market momentum measures the Taiwan weighted index's position relative to its medium-term trend and reflects chasing pressure in local equities.
twMarketMomentum.detailDescription: This indicator looks at how far Taiwan's market sits above or below its trend line to judge whether prices have become stretched. When the index stays well above trend, buyers are chasing and sentiment is typically optimistic. When the index is far below trend, pessimism is more dominant and the market is usually in defense mode. It works as a sentiment read because market mood eventually shows up as price extension away from trend.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: When Taiwan's market is clearly above its medium-term moving average, sentiment is usually greedier. When it is clearly below the average, sentiment is usually more fearful.

etaDeviation189d.shortDescription: Effective trading accounts measures actively trading Taiwan accounts versus their 189-day trend, highlighting shifts in participation.
etaDeviation189d.detailDescription: This indicator compares the current count of actively trading accounts to its 189-day trend, so it reveals whether participation is unusually heated or cooled relative to the longer trajectory. When the reading sits well above trend, more accounts are being drawn in and sentiment is generally risk-on. When it sits well below trend, participation is thinning and risk appetite is fading. It works as a sentiment read because expansion or contraction in the crowd's participation versus trend often leads broader shifts in attention and risk appetite.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: Readings above the 189-day trend indicate heated participation and greed. Readings below the trend indicate cooling participation and fear.

twVix.shortDescription: The Taiwan VIX is the TAIFEX implied volatility index on TAIEX options and reads the cost of hedging Taiwan equities.
twVix.detailDescription: TW VIX essentially measures how much investors are willing to pay for downside protection, which ties directly to fear. When TW VIX rises, expected volatility and hedging demand are increasing and the market is tense. When it falls, hedging demand cools and risk appetite rebuilds. It works as a sentiment read because changes in the cost of protection typically reveal trader anxiety earlier than price itself.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: A rising TW VIX indicates growing fear and hedging demand. A falling TW VIX indicates recovering risk appetite and greedier positioning.

twPcr.shortDescription: The TAIEX options Put/Call ratio compares put activity (or open interest) to call activity, revealing the hedging-versus-speculation balance.
twPcr.detailDescription: PCR puts put demand and call demand on the same scale. When PCR is elevated, hedging dominates and fear is widespread — which historically clusters near durable lows. When PCR is depressed, call demand dominates and speculation is heating up, which often maps to overheated conditions. It works as a sentiment read because options positioning reflects the direction in which traders are actually willing to commit capital.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: Elevated PCR (extreme hedging) typically points to washed-out sentiment and potential rebounds. Depressed PCR points to speculative, risk-on conditions.

usdTwd.shortDescription: The USD/TWD exchange rate tracks capital-flow pressure in and out of Taiwan and links to foreign-investor risk appetite for Taiwan equities.
usdTwd.detailDescription: When the TWD weakens (USD/TWD rises), foreign capital is typically flowing out and hedging demand is rising — a headwind for Taiwan equities. When the TWD strengthens (USD/TWD falls), capital is returning and global risk appetite for Taiwan assets is generally improving. It works as a sentiment read because FX reflects both international risk posture and the allocation preference toward Taiwan assets, and often leads equity sentiment.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: A rising USD/TWD points to outflows and fear. A falling USD/TWD points to inflows and greed.

marginMaintenanceRatio.shortDescription: The margin maintenance ratio tracks the financial health of Taiwan margin accounts and is the primary read on retail leverage stress.
marginMaintenanceRatio.detailDescription: A higher margin maintenance ratio means margin positions are safer and further from forced-liquidation thresholds, while a falling ratio means margin losses are widening and forced-selling pressure is rising. During sharp drawdowns this ratio often reveals that retail leverage has reached its breaking point faster than the index does. It works as a sentiment read because the safety buffer of margin traders directly reflects the willingness and capacity of Taiwan retail to carry risk.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: A higher margin maintenance ratio indicates safer retail leverage and greedier sentiment. A lower ratio indicates mounting margin-call pressure and fear.

finiFutures.shortDescription: Foreign-institution net futures open interest tracks the net long/short TAIEX futures position held by foreign institutions, reflecting their directional bet on the Taiwan market.
finiFutures.detailDescription: Foreign institutions are one of the most influential capital groups in Taiwan, and their net long or short TAIEX futures position reveals hedging or offensive intent more directly than cash-market flows. When net longs expand to historically elevated levels, sentiment is generally optimistic and the setup often coincides with interim tops. When net shorts deepen, foreign money is defensive and pessimism is usually already priced in. It works as a sentiment read because futures positioning represents actual capital carrying directional risk.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: Very large foreign net longs often mark top risk (contrarian fear signal). Very deep foreign net shorts often mark exhausted pessimism.

marketBreadth.shortDescription: Market breadth compares the number of advancing versus declining Taiwan stocks to measure how widely a rally or decline is participating.
marketBreadth.detailDescription: When the index rallies it does not mean every stock is rallying, and breadth tells you exactly that. Strong breadth means advancing names are widespread and the rally is broad — a hallmark of greed. Weakening breadth means even a rising index is being carried by a handful of heavyweights, which quietly warns of internal exhaustion. It works as a sentiment read because breadth reflects whether the broader crowd is aligned with the trend, not just the headline index.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: Broadening market breadth signals broad participation and greed. Narrowing breadth signals concentrated leadership and underlying fear.

vixMA50.shortDescription: The VIX Index (Volatility Index), often referred to as the 'Fear Gauge,' measures the market's expectation of 30-day forward-looking volatility of the S&P 500 Index. Here, the 50-day moving average of the VIX is calculated to observe long-term trends in market sentiment.
vixMA50.detailDescription: VIX is essentially a measure of how much investors are willing to pay for protection, which ties closely to fear. Here we use the 50-day average instead of one-day spikes, so the signal is better for medium-term sentiment pressure rather than short-lived headlines. When VIX MA50 rises, the market is staying tense, defensive, and concerned about broader risk. When it falls, panic is cooling and risk appetite is beginning to recover.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: An ascending VIX 50-day moving average indicates rising market fear and increased demand for hedging. Conversely, a descending VIX 50-day moving average suggests a relatively calm market, higher investor risk appetite, and a shift in market sentiment towards greed.

safeHaven.shortDescription: The Safe Haven Demand indicator compares the difference between the total return of stocks (risk asset) and US Treasury bonds (safe-haven asset)over the past 20 trading days. It reflects the extent of fund flows into safe-haven assets.
safeHaven.detailDescription: This indicator compares whether money has recently preferred equities or safe-haven assets like Treasuries. When safe havens clearly outperform, the market is usually pulling back from risk and leaning defensive. When equities outperform, investors are more willing to take risk and sentiment is more optimistic. It works because flows themselves reflect risk appetite: where money is moving often tells you whether the market is in offense or defense mode.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: When bond returns significantly outperform stock returns (low indicator value), it indicates investors are flocking to safe-haven assets, suggesting market fear. When stock returns significantly outperform bond returns (high indicator value), it indicates higher risk appetite and fund flows into risk assets, suggesting market greed.

junkBond.shortDescription: The yield spread between junk bonds (high-yield corporate bonds) and investment-grade corporate bonds reflects the market's attitude towards credit risk. Junk bonds are riskier and typically have higher yields.
junkBond.detailDescription: The junk bond spread shows whether investors are willing to hold lower-quality corporate debt. When spreads widen, investors are demanding more compensation for credit risk, which usually means fear is rising. When spreads tighten, investors are becoming more comfortable with risk and sentiment is often leaning toward greed. It works as a sentiment indicator because credit markets reflect willingness to take risk very directly, not just price direction.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: When the spread widens (high indicator value), it means investors demand higher risk compensation to hold junk bonds. This usually happens when the market worries about economic prospects or tightening liquidity, indicating market fear. When the spread narrows (low indicator value), it means investors' risk tolerance increases, indicating market greed.

cotIndex.shortDescription: The COT Index (Commitments of Traders Index), based on the weekly report from the CFTC, measures the net position (longs minus shorts) of large speculators (often considered more informed traders) in the S&P 500 futures market relative to historical levels.
cotIndex.detailDescription: This indicator looks at whether speculative futures positions are tilted long or short, which effectively shows where leveraged money is standing. When speculators become heavily long, the market consensus may already be very optimistic. When positioning turns heavily short, pessimism is building. It works as a sentiment gauge because large speculative players are not just expressing opinions, they are backing them with positions, and crowded positioning often signals crowded trades.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: A COT Index near 100% indicates large speculators' net long positions are at historical highs, suggesting the market might be overly bullish and leaning towards extreme greed. An index near 0% indicates net short positions are at historical highs (or net longs are extremely low), suggesting the market might be overly bearish and leaning towards extreme fear.

naaimIndex.shortDescription: The NAAIM Exposure Index (National Association of Active Investment Managers Exposure Index) surveys its members (active investment managers) weekly on their current equity market exposure level (0% = no stocks, 100% = fully invested, >100% = leveraged).
naaimIndex.detailDescription: This indicator shows how much equity exposure active investment managers are actually carrying. When exposure is very high, professional investors are broadly confident and optimism is already widespread. When exposure falls sharply, professional money is pulling risk back. It works as a sentiment measure because real portfolio exposure is more revealing than commentary: whether managers are willing to put actual capital to work tells you a lot about market confidence.

sections.title: Interpretation Method
sections.content: An extremely high exposure index (e.g., near or above 100%) indicates fund managers are generally bullish and actively holding stocks, suggesting market greed. An extremely low exposure index (e.g., near 0% or negative, indicating short positions) indicates managers are generally bearish and reducing stock holdings, suggesting market fear.

tips.tip1: When the indicator shows extreme fear (0-20), it's typically a good buying opportunity
tips.tip2: When the indicator shows extreme greed (80-100), be cautious about chasing highs and consider profit-taking
tips.tip3: Observe multiple timeframes to avoid being misled by short-term fluctuations

faq.q1: What is the SIO Market Sentiment Indicator?
faq.a1: The SIO Market Sentiment Indicator is a tool designed to measure overall market sentiment. It analyzes multiple technical and fundamental indicators to assess the levels of fear and greed in the market.
faq.q2: How is this different from the 'CNN Fear & Greed Index' or the 'BofA Bull & Bear Indicator'?
faq.a2: The SIO indicator is designed for long-term allocation, with logic that benchmarks against the institutional-grade BofA indicator. While the CNN index is sensitive, it focuses more on the short term and can struggle to identify structural bottoms in long cycles. Our goal with SIO is to create a professional tool that aids long-term decision-making, aiming to match the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator's ability to catch long-term market turning points.
faq.q3: What does the 0 to 100 score mean? How do I interpret it?
faq.a3: The score represents the current market state's relative position in history. It ranges from 0 to 100: 0-20 is Extreme Fear, 21-40 is Fear, 41-60 is Neutral, 61-80 is Greed, and 81-100 is Extreme Greed. It's important to note that a high score doesn't mean an immediate crash; greedy sentiment can often persist for a long time.
faq.q4: How often is the data updated?
faq.a4: The composite score updates whenever the individual indicators update, so basically, it updates every day.
faq.q5: How can you compare different indicators, like the 'VIX' and 'AAII Retail Sentiment', together?
faq.a5: We mainly use the statistical Z-Score normalization method. Since different indicators have different units (e.g., VIX is volatility, AAII is a net ratio), the Z-Score allows us to convert all of them into a unified statistical measure.
faq.q6: For weekly data (like COT reports), how does the indicator handle 'publication delays' to avoid look-ahead bias?
faq.a6: We strictly enforce 'Point-in-Time' calibration during calculation to avoid 'peeking into the future.' For example, the CFTC COT report comes out on Friday but covers data up to Tuesday. So, our system forces a lag in the calculation. This means when backtesting a historical Wednesday or Thursday, we restore the state where that week's data wasn't available yet, simulating the information gap in a real trading environment to ensure credibility.
faq.q7: Has the strategy of buying under 15 and selling over 96 gone through Out-of-Sample stress testing?
faq.a7: Yes, the backtest uses rigorous 'Walk-Forward Validation.' I deliberately locked the model parameters using data from before 2019 and set 2020 to 2026 as the 'blind test' period. The results show that even through the extreme environments of the COVID-19 crash and the 2022 stock/bond double dip, the strategy still delivered better risk-adjusted returns than the broader market during the blind test, with a significantly lower max drawdown than the S&P 500.
faq.q8: Why do you suggest buying when it drops below 15? Past crashes went below 5, can't I just wait for 5?
faq.a8: To avoid missing out on mid-term pullbacks, we suggest a 'batch entry' strategy. While historical disasters (like the 2008 Financial Crisis or 2020 Pandemic) do push the indicator below 5, those are extremely rare. Some mid-sized corrections might bottom out around 8-12 (like the 2011 Euro Debt Crisis or the 2025 Trade War). If you insist on waiting for < 5, you might miss the entry entirely. Therefore, the best strategy is a 'Two-Stage Entry': Stage 1 (< 15): Deploy 50% to ensure you catch the rebound. Stage 2 (< 5): If a systemic crash happens, invest the remaining 50%. Backtests prove that this 'half now, half later' approach strikes the best balance between risk and reward.
faq.q9: If the indicator shows 'Extreme Greed (96+)', should I sell everything or go short immediately?
faq.a9: That's not recommended. When the indicator enters the >96 Extreme Greed zone, the market often stays greedy for a while. Selling everything might make you miss the main rally, and shorting is extremely risky. We suggest you stop chasing highs at this point and moderately take profits in batches.
faq.q10: Why is the composite score up at 90+ when none of the individual indicators have reached extreme greed?
faq.a10: Because the model values 'breadth.' When retail investors, whales, the hedging market, and the bond market all turn optimistic *at the same time*, that consensus is actually rarer historically than just one indicator hitting an extreme. This high level of consistency pushes up the composite percentile ranking, alerting investors to potential structural risks.

faq.q1: What is the SIO Taiwan Sentiment Indicator?
faq.a1: The SIO Taiwan Sentiment Indicator measures the overall sentiment of the Taiwan stock market. It combines nine TAIEX-specific signals — options-implied volatility, foreign-institution futures positioning, margin maintenance ratio and more — into a single 0-to-100 score, helping long-term investors identify when Taiwan's market has entered an extreme zone.
faq.q2: How is this different from the 'CNN Fear & Greed Index' or the 'BofA Bull & Bear Indicator'?
faq.a2: Both CNN and BofA indicators are built for the US market, using VIX, Put/Call Ratio, AAII and other US-specific data that can't capture what moves Taiwan stocks — foreign-institution futures positioning, margin maintenance ratio, margin-to-short ratio and USD/TWD. The SIO Taiwan Fear & Greed Index is a TAIEX-customized version that aggregates nine Taiwan-native signals: options-implied volatility, retail and foreign positioning, FX pressure and market breadth. It keeps the same long-horizon allocation logic as the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator, but properly reflects Taiwan's capital flow and sentiment structure.
faq.q3: What does the 0 to 100 score mean? How do I interpret it?
faq.a3: The score represents Taiwan's sentiment in its historical context. 0-20 is Extreme Fear, 21-40 Fear, 41-60 Neutral, 61-80 Greed, 81-100 Extreme Greed. A high score doesn't mean an immediate reversal — TAIEX can stay elevated while foreign institutions keep buying. The signal worth watching is when multiple indicators approach extremes simultaneously.
faq.q4: How often is the data updated?
faq.a4: The composite score updates as its components update. Daily-frequency signals (options volatility, margin maintenance, index momentum) refresh every trading session; weekly data (foreign futures positioning, effective trading accounts) refreshes on its release schedule. In practice, the composite score moves every trading day.
faq.q5: How can indicators with completely different units — like options volatility and margin maintenance ratio — be combined?
faq.a5: All signals are normalized using Z-scores. Volatility is a percentage, margin maintenance is a ratio, foreign futures are contract counts — the Z-score converts each to its relative position against its own historical distribution, letting them be weighted and aggregated on a comparable scale.
faq.q6: How does the indicator avoid look-ahead bias for weekly or post-close data, like foreign futures positioning?
faq.a6: We enforce Point-in-Time calibration throughout the calculation. Foreign-institution futures data is released after market close; margin and short-interest balances are released the following day. During backtesting the system reconstructs the information state that was actually available at each moment, adding the corresponding lag, to prevent 'peeking into the future.'
faq.q7: Has the below-15 buy / above-96 trim strategy gone through out-of-sample stress testing?
faq.a7: Yes. We use Walk-Forward Validation: model parameters are locked to pre-2019 Taiwan data, with 2020 through 2026 as a blind test period. Across the 2020 pandemic crash, the 2022 rate-hike drawdown, and the 2024 TAIEX all-time highs, the strategy delivered better risk-adjusted returns than buy-and-hold TAIEX, with materially lower maximum drawdown.
faq.q8: At what score should I start entering? Is there one best entry point?
faq.a8: There isn't one best score. Historically, larger TAIEX corrections have tended to push the indicator below 15, but whether any given correction reaches that level — and how much further it might go — isn't predictable. Some pullbacks stabilize near 15; others grind all the way into single digits. How you stage entries should therefore depend on your own risk tolerance, time horizon and position size: a conservative investor may begin small tranches earlier (around 15-20), while a more aggressive one may wait for deeper readings. The point isn't to wait for a specific number; it's to decide in advance — based on the drawdown you can actually sit through — how you'll scale in, so that discipline rather than emotion drives each entry.
faq.q9: If the indicator hits Extreme Greed (96+), should I sell everything or short TAIEX immediately?
faq.a9: Not recommended. When the score enters the >96 zone while foreign institutions are still net buyers and margin has not yet overheated, TAIEX can stay strong for a while. Liquidating risks missing the main leg up, and shorting carries outsized downside. A more reasonable approach is to review your risk exposure and, based on your allocation plan, consider trimming in tranches.
faq.q10: Why is the composite score above 90 when no individual indicator has reached an extreme?
faq.a10: Because the model reads breadth, not just peaks. When retail margin, foreign futures longs, call-skewed options positioning, market breadth and momentum all tilt bullish at the same time, that cross-signal consensus is historically rarer in Taiwan than any single series hitting its own extreme. The simultaneous agreement pushes the composite percentile up — a warning that structural risk is accumulating.

jsonLd.name: LOHAS Five-Line Analysis
jsonLd.description: The LOHAS Five-Line fits a trend to the last 3.5 years of prices and adds two lines either side, marking how far price usually strays from that trend. The closer to the outer edge, the further price sits from its long-term trend: the top line shows as "Extreme Greed", the bottom as "Extreme Fear". Read alongside the faster-moving LOHAS Channel, it indicates whether the short term is overheated or oversold. It is a way to see where a stock or index ETF sits in its long-term trend — a reference point, not a standalone basis for buying or selling.

sd.title: What do the five lines mean?
sd.point1: The middle line is a trend fitted to the last 3.5 years of prices. The two lines either side mark how far price usually strays from it; the outermost pair is already unusual territory.
sd.point2: The closer to the outer edge, the further price sits from its long-term trend. Testing shows this chart alone is not enough — it is worth reading alongside the LOHAS Channel.
sd.point3: Touching the top line is what shows as "Extreme Greed" above. It happens roughly one trading day in ten — less rare than most people assume.
sd.point4: Touching the bottom line shows as "Extreme Fear". On its own it says little; it matters when the LOHAS Channel turns "Short-term oversold" at the same time.

ulband.title: What is the LOHAS Channel, and how is it different?
ulband.point1: The LOHAS Channel is built from the highs and lows of the last 20 weeks, so it reacts faster than the Five-Line and describes the short term.
ulband.point2: Price above the upper band shows as "Short-term overheated" above.
ulband.point3: Price below the lower band shows as "Short-term oversold" above.

bofaBullBear.pageTitle: What is the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator and how do you read it?
bofaBullBear.pageDescription: A full guide to the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator: a 0-to-10 contrarian sentiment gauge where above 8 signals selling and below 2 signals buying, built from six flow and positioning inputs. Includes the latest reading, a historical chart and how to interpret it.
bofaBullBear.keywords: bofa bull bear indicator,BofA Bull and Bear,BofA sentiment indicator,Hartnett,Flow Show,contrarian indicator,market sentiment indicator,stock sentiment tracker
bofaBullBear.heading: What is the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator and how do you read it?
bofaBullBear.lede: The BofA Bull & Bear Indicator is a weekly sentiment gauge from Bank of America, scoring investor positioning from 0 to 10. It is read contrarily: the higher the number, the more people are already betting the same way, which leaves less force behind any further move.
bofaBullBear.whatItIsTitle: What is the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator?
bofaBullBear.whatItIs: The gauge comes from the BofA Investment Strategy team led by chief strategist Michael Hartnett, and updates each week with The Flow Show, typically Thursday evening to Friday US time. It ignores price action and instead aggregates six measures of where money is flowing and how investors are positioned, converting each to a percentile before combining them into a 0-to-10 score. The underlying data covers global fund flows, BofA's own survey of fund managers, futures market positioning and global equity breadth.
bofaBullBear.howToReadTitle: How do you read the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator?
bofaBullBear.howToRead: It is a contrarian gauge, so extreme readings mean most participants are already on one side. BofA defines above 8.0 as extreme bullish and below 2.0 as extreme bearish.

bands.meaning: Extreme bullish. BofA treats this as a contrarian sell signal, indicating a crowded long position rather than a forecast of decline.
Neutral range. The gauge carries no clear signal on its own and needs other context.
Extreme bearish. BofA treats this as a contrarian buy signal, usually seen after heavy outflows and capitulation.

bofaBullBear.componentsTitle: Which six components make up the BofA Bull & Bear Indicator?
bofaBullBear.componentsIntro: Each component is expressed as a percentile from 0% to 100%, then combined into the headline score. BofA publishes all six alongside the reading, so the breakdown shows what drove any given week.

components.name: Hedge Fund Positioning
components.note: How much equity exposure hedge funds are carrying.

components.name: Equity Flow
components.note: Money moving into equity funds, measured by EPFR, a firm that tracks fund flows worldwide.

components.name: Bond Flow
components.note: Money moving into bond funds, used to gauge appetite for risk.

components.name: Credit Market Technicals
components.note: Supply, demand and spread conditions in corporate credit.

components.name: Global Stock Index Breadth
components.note: How many global markets are in an uptrend.

components.name: FMS Positioning
components.note: Actual allocations reported in BofA's monthly survey of global fund managers.

bofaBullBear.history: The series goes back to 2002. We have tracked it continuously since November 2023, over which it has ranged from 1.4 to 9.7. Readings above 8.0 are historically uncommon; the 9.7 print in August 2026 was the highest since 2021. Note that the gauge can sit in extreme territory for weeks or longer, so reaching an extreme and the market turning are two different events.
bofaBullBear.relationToSioTitle: How it differs from the SIO Fear & Greed Index
bofaBullBear.relationToSio: The BofA gauge carries two practical limitations. First, the underlying report is paid research that retail investors cannot access, so the number reaches the public only through financial media, and some weeks nobody reports it. Second, it updates once a week, so a mid-week move leaves the gauge stuck on last week's reading. The SIO Fear & Greed Index addresses both: it updates every trading day from public market data covering volatility, put/call ratios, credit spreads and momentum, with a complete series and no gaps. The two use different inputs, so gaps between them are normal, and those gaps usually say more than either number alone.

bofaBullBear.source: BofA Global Investment Strategy. Readings are published with The Flow Show.

cnnFearGreed.pageTitle: What is the CNN Fear & Greed Index and how do you read it?
cnnFearGreed.pageDescription: A full guide to the CNN Fear & Greed Index: a 0-to-100 sentiment gauge where below 25 is extreme fear and above 75 is extreme greed, built from seven market inputs. Includes the latest reading, how to interpret it and its known limits.
cnnFearGreed.keywords: cnn fear and greed index,fear greed index,CNN Fear Greed,market sentiment index,extreme fear,extreme greed,stock sentiment tracker
cnnFearGreed.heading: What is the CNN Fear & Greed Index and how do you read it?
cnnFearGreed.lede: The CNN Fear & Greed Index is the most widely followed sentiment gauge for US stocks, describing on a 0-to-100 scale whether investors currently lean fearful or greedy. Lower means more panic, higher means more optimism.
cnnFearGreed.whatItIsTitle: What is the CNN Fear & Greed Index?
cnnFearGreed.whatItIs: CNN builds the index from seven market inputs: where prices sit relative to their moving average, the balance of new highs against new lows, volume in advancing versus declining stocks, the ratio of put to call options, the spread between junk and investment grade bonds, market volatility, and recent stock returns against bonds. Each is rescaled and averaged into a 0-to-100 score, updated every trading day.
cnnFearGreed.howToReadTitle: How do you read the CNN Fear & Greed Index?
cnnFearGreed.howToRead: CNN divides the range into five bands. Most people use it contrarily, watching for entries during extreme fear and for risk during extreme greed.

bands.meaning: Extreme Fear. The market is in panic, usually alongside heavy selling.
Fear. Investors are leaning defensive.
Neutral. Buyers and sellers are evenly matched.
Greed. Risk appetite is rising.
Extreme Greed. Strong willingness to chase prices, which stretches valuations.

cnnFearGreed.historyTitle: Historical range of the CNN Fear & Greed Index
cnnFearGreed.history: The index runs from 0 to 100. Our complete daily record starts in 2021, over which it has reached a low of 2.9 (8 April 2025) and a high of 83.0 (19 December 2023). Extreme fear typically appears during fast declines, extreme greed after sustained rallies.
cnnFearGreed.relationToSioTitle: How it differs from the SIO Fear & Greed Index
cnnFearGreed.relationToSio: The CNN index leans short term. Most of its seven inputs look at changes over the past days to weeks, so during a decline it drops into extreme fear early, then pins to the floor while the market keeps falling, losing the ability to discriminate. The SIO Fear & Greed Index standardises each input against more than a decade of history, so even at extremes it still separates ordinary fear from genuinely rare fear. Reading both together keeps short-term signals in perspective.

cnnFearGreed.source: CNN Business. Updated every trading day.
cnnFearGreed.componentsTitle: Which seven components make up the CNN Fear & Greed Index?
cnnFearGreed.componentsIntro: Each component is rescaled to 0-100 and averaged into the headline reading, so the breakdown shows what is driving the score today.

components.name: Market Momentum
components.note: Where the S&P 500 sits relative to its 125-day moving average.

components.name: Stock Price Strength
components.note: The balance of 52-week highs against 52-week lows.

components.name: Stock Price Breadth
components.note: Volume in advancing stocks versus declining stocks.

components.name: Put/Call Options
components.note: Put volume against call volume, a read on hedging demand.

components.name: Market Volatility
components.note: Where VIX sits relative to its 50-day moving average.

components.name: Junk Bond Demand
components.note: The yield spread between junk and investment grade bonds; a narrowing spread means more appetite for risk.

components.name: Safe Haven Demand
components.note: Recent stock returns against bond returns.

aaiiSurvey.pageTitle: What is the AAII Sentiment Survey and how do you read it?
aaiiSurvey.pageDescription: A full guide to the AAII Sentiment Survey: a weekly poll of US individual investors on the next six months, with the Bull-Bear Spread as the headline number. Includes the latest reading, how to interpret it and its known limits.
aaiiSurvey.keywords: aaii sentiment survey,AAII bull bear spread,retail investor sentiment,individual investor sentiment,market sentiment indicator
aaiiSurvey.heading: What is the AAII Sentiment Survey and how do you read it?
aaiiSurvey.lede: The AAII Sentiment Survey is a weekly poll of US individual investors asking where they think the stock market goes over the next six months. The most quoted figure is the Bull-Bear Spread, the share who are bullish minus the share who are bearish.
aaiiSurvey.whatItIsTitle: What is the AAII Sentiment Survey?
aaiiSurvey.whatItIs: AAII is the American Association of Individual Investors, which has polled its members weekly since 1987 with a single question: will the market be up, down or flat over the next six months. The three shares sum to 100%, and bullish minus bearish gives the spread. It is one of the few sentiment gauges that asks people directly; most others infer mood from trading data.
aaiiSurvey.howToReadTitle: How do you read the AAII Bull-Bear Spread?
aaiiSurvey.howToRead: A positive spread means more bulls than bears. The long-run average sits around plus 6 to 7 points, so the sign alone says little; what matters is how far it sits from that norm. Most people read it contrarily.

bands.meaning: Retail investors are clearly optimistic. Historically seen after a rally has run for a while.
Close to the normal range, limited signal.
Retail investors are clearly pessimistic. Historically seen after sharp declines and read as a contrarian marker.

aaiiSurvey.historyTitle: Historical range of the AAII Bull-Bear Spread
aaiiSurvey.history: The survey has run since July 1987, making it the longest series we track with more than two thousand weekly readings. The spread spends most of its time between minus 20 and plus 20 points, with an all-time low of -54.0 (19 October 1990) and a high of +62.8 (26 June 2003). Readings beyond plus or minus 30 are comparatively rare and usually coincide with violent moves in the market.
aaiiSurvey.relationToSioTitle: How it differs from the SIO Fear & Greed Index
aaiiSurvey.relationToSio: AAII carries two built-in limits. It is a survey answered by self-selecting members, so the sample shifts each week and the raw number is noisy. It also asks what people think, and what people think often differs from what they trade. The SIO Fear & Greed Index treats AAII as one component, smoothed and standardised before being combined with seven other inputs, so no single survey dominates the reading.

aaiiSurvey.source: American Association of Individual Investors (AAII). Updated weekly.

naaimExposure.pageTitle: What is the NAAIM Exposure Index and how do you read it?
naaimExposure.pageDescription: A full guide to the NAAIM Exposure Index: a weekly survey of US active investment managers reporting their actual equity exposure, ranging from -200 to +200. Includes the latest reading, how to interpret it and its known limits.
naaimExposure.keywords: naaim exposure index,NAAIM,active manager exposure,fund manager positioning,market sentiment indicator
naaimExposure.heading: What is the NAAIM Exposure Index and how do you read it?
naaimExposure.lede: The NAAIM Exposure Index surveys US active investment managers each week on how much equity exposure they are actually carrying. It reflects what professionals have done rather than what they say, which makes it a useful counterpart to survey-based gauges.
naaimExposure.whatItIsTitle: What is the NAAIM Exposure Index?
naaimExposure.whatItIs: NAAIM is the National Association of Active Investment Managers. Each Wednesday it asks members for their current equity exposure. A reading of 100 means fully long, 0 means flat, and negative values mean net short, with a theoretical range from -200 to +200. Because it asks about actual positions, it measures behaviour rather than opinion.
naaimExposure.howToReadTitle: How do you read the NAAIM Exposure Index?
naaimExposure.howToRead: This gauge follows positioning directly: higher means managers are more committed to equities. Extremes are usually read contrarily, since a fully invested manager has little dry powder left.

bands.meaning: Close to fully invested. Managers are heavily committed with limited room to add.
The common range, limited signal.
Heavily reduced or flat. Historically seen during market panics.

naaimExposure.historyTitle: Historical range of the NAAIM Exposure Index
naaimExposure.history: Our record starts in July 2006. The index spends most of its time between 40 and 90, with a low of -3.6 (5 October 2011, meaning net short overall) and a high of 120.6 (13 December 2017, meaning leveraged long). Keep in mind it produces one number per week, so it lags when the market moves sharply mid-week.
naaimExposure.relationToSioTitle: How it differs from the SIO Fear & Greed Index
naaimExposure.relationToSio: The NAAIM sample covers a few dozen active managers, small enough that one firm changing its book can move the number visibly. It also updates only weekly, which leaves a lag when you are trying to read the market today. The SIO Fear & Greed Index updates every trading day and standardises NAAIM alongside seven other inputs, so swings in any single survey do not get amplified.
naaimExposure.relationToSioCta: View the SIO US Fear & Greed Index
naaimExposure.source: National Association of Active Investment Managers (NAAIM). Updated weekly.

cboePutCall.pageTitle: What is the CBOE Put/Call Ratio and how do you read it?
cboePutCall.pageDescription: A full guide to the CBOE Put/Call Ratio: the ratio of put to call option volume, where higher readings signal stronger demand for downside protection. Includes the latest reading, how to interpret it and its known limits.
cboePutCall.keywords: cboe put call ratio,put call ratio,PCR,options ratio,hedging demand,market sentiment indicator
cboePutCall.heading: What is the CBOE Put/Call Ratio and how do you read it?
cboePutCall.lede: The Put/Call Ratio divides put option volume by call option volume. Puts are typically bought for protection or to bet on declines while calls express upside views, so the ratio shows whether investors are protecting positions or chasing gains.
cboePutCall.whatItIsTitle: What is the CBOE Put/Call Ratio?
cboePutCall.whatItIs: CBOE is the Chicago Board Options Exchange, one of the largest options venues in the world. It publishes daily put and call volume, and dividing one by the other gives the ratio. A reading above 1 means more puts traded than calls that day, which typically happens when markets are tense. Because the daily figure swings hard, it is usually smoothed over several days before use.
cboePutCall.howToReadTitle: How do you read the CBOE Put/Call Ratio?
cboePutCall.howToRead: This is a contrarian gauge. A high ratio means heavy buying of protection and bearish positioning; a low ratio means the market is discounting risk. Extremes often cluster near turning points.

bands.meaning: Put volume exceeds call volume, showing clear demand for hedges and bearish sentiment.
The common range.
Calls clearly outweigh puts, indicating low awareness of risk.

cboePutCall.historyTitle: Historical range of the CBOE Put/Call Ratio
cboePutCall.history: Our five-day average record starts in November 2006, ranging from a low of 0.37 (19 January 2021) to a high of 1.47 (28 December 2022). Note that the options market has changed substantially: the rise of very short-dated contracts has altered the composition of volume, so comparing today directly against readings from long ago deserves caution.
cboePutCall.relationToSioTitle: How it differs from the SIO Fear & Greed Index
cboePutCall.relationToSio: The daily ratio is noisy enough to swing from 0.6 to 1.2 within one week, which misleads if read raw. It also reflects only the options market, saying nothing about cash equities, bonds or fund flows. The SIO Fear & Greed Index smooths it and standardises it alongside seven other inputs, covering what options alone cannot see.

cboePutCall.source: Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE). Updated every trading day.

cotSp500.pageTitle: What is the COT report and S&P 500 speculative positioning?
cotSp500.pageDescription: A full guide to the Commitments of Traders report: weekly US futures positioning data broken out by participant type, with S&P 500 speculative net positioning widely used as a sentiment gauge. Includes how to interpret it and its known limits.
cotSp500.keywords: COT report,commitments of traders,speculative net positioning,S&P 500 futures,CFTC,market sentiment indicator
cotSp500.heading: What is the COT report and S&P 500 speculative positioning?
cotSp500.lede: The Commitments of Traders report is weekly positioning data from the US futures regulator, breaking the market down by participant type. The net long or short position held by speculative accounts is widely used to gauge sentiment.
cotSp500.whatItIsTitle: What is the Commitments of Traders (COT) report?
cotSp500.whatItIs: The report is published by the CFTC, the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates futures markets. It comes out every Friday covering positions as of the preceding Tuesday, splitting participants into commercial hedgers, speculative money and small traders. The reading used here expresses speculative net positioning (leveraged funds plus asset managers) and hedger net positioning each as a share of total open interest, then takes the difference, producing a figure comparable across time.
cotSp500.howToReadTitle: How do you read S&P 500 speculative positioning?
cotSp500.howToRead: Hedgers are the counterparty to speculative money, so the two sit on opposite sides by construction and taking the difference amplifies the signal. A high reading means the two camps are far apart with speculators leaning long; a low reading means the reverse. Extremes are usually read contrarily.

bands.meaning: Speculators are clearly long relative to hedgers, with the two camps far apart.
The common state, limited signal.
Speculators are clearly short relative to hedgers.

cotSp500.historyTitle: Historical range of COT positioning data
cotSp500.history: Our record starts in June 2006. Three things are worth noting: the report carries a three-day lag, with Friday publication covering Tuesday positions; the CFTC revised contract classifications around 2021, so comparisons spanning that point need care; and asset managers are counted on the speculative side even though many such accounts run structurally long allocations, which is worth bearing in mind when reading extremes.
cotSp500.relationToSioTitle: How it differs from the SIO Fear & Greed Index
cotSp500.relationToSio: COT carries two limits. It publishes weekly, and its as-of date sits three days before publication, so what you see is always days old. It also covers only futures, saying nothing about cash equities or options. Because it is a spread between speculative and hedger positioning, extremes reflect both sides at once and are easy to misread in isolation. The SIO Fear & Greed Index updates every trading day and standardises COT alongside seven other inputs, so neither the lag nor the definitional quirks dominate the overall read.

cotSp500.source: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Published every Friday.

taiwanFearGreed.pageTitle: What is the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index and how do you read it?
taiwanFearGreed.pageDescription: A full guide to the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index: a 0-to-100 sentiment gauge for Taiwan equities built from local data including TAIFEX options volatility, put/call ratio, margin ratios and market breadth, updated every trading day.
taiwanFearGreed.keywords: taiwan fear and greed index,taiwan stock sentiment,TAIEX sentiment,taiwan VIX,TAIFEX,margin ratio,taiwan market sentiment
taiwanFearGreed.heading: What is the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index and how do you read it?
taiwanFearGreed.lede: The Taiwan Fear & Greed Index describes on a 0-to-100 scale whether Taiwan equity investors currently lean fearful or greedy. It is calculated entirely from local market data covering options volatility, margin financing, foreign investor positioning and market breadth, updated every trading day.
taiwanFearGreed.whatItIsTitle: What is the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index?
taiwanFearGreed.whatItIs: Nearly every well-known sentiment gauge is built for US equities, which leaves Taiwan investors applying tools designed for a different market structure. Retail participation, the margin financing system and the weight of foreign institutional flows all differ from the US, so borrowing US readings directly invites misreads. This index uses Taiwan data instead: TAIFEX options volatility, the options put/call ratio, margin maintenance and short-to-margin ratios, market breadth, foreign futures positioning, the exchange rate and TAIEX momentum, each standardised against its own long history before being combined.
taiwanFearGreed.howToReadTitle: How do you read the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index?
taiwanFearGreed.howToRead: Lower means more panic, higher means more optimism. Because each input is standardised over a long window, an extreme reading means extreme relative to more than two decades of history rather than just the past few months.

bands.meaning: Extreme fear. The market is in panic and margin balances typically contract sharply.
Fear. Sentiment leans defensive.
Neutral. Buyers and sellers are evenly matched.
Greed. Risk appetite is rising.
Extreme greed. Strong willingness to chase prices.

taiwanFearGreed.historyTitle: Historical range of the Taiwan Fear & Greed Index
taiwanFearGreed.history: The series goes back to July 2001 with more than six thousand daily readings, covering two decades of Taiwan bull and bear cycles and reaching both ends of the 0-to-100 range. Note that TAIFEX options volatility data begins only in November 2016, so readings before that rest on the remaining components, which is worth bearing in mind when interpreting early values.
taiwanFearGreed.relationToSioTitle: How Taiwan sentiment differs from US sentiment
taiwanFearGreed.relationToSio: Taiwan and US sentiment frequently move out of step. Taiwan is heavily shaped by foreign institutional flows, the exchange rate and the electronics cycle, none of which appear in US gauges. Watching both reveals whether money is de-risking globally or repositioning within a single market.
